title: Tryambakam yajāmahe: released from death like the ripe fruit from its stalk
theme: The three-eyed one, fragrant, who increases prosperity, is worshipped; the speaker asks to be released from death as a ripe cucumber is from its stalk, and not from immortality.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «लौकिकवैदिकपुष्टिं वर्धयतीति» — who increases prosperity, worldly and Vedic
The anonymous commentator: «कर्कट्यादेः फलं» — the fruit of the cucumber and the like

words.role: main verb of the second line
negates the release from what follows

sandhi.type: t before a nasal; visarga after o before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: bandhanāt before m becomes bandhanān; mṛtyoḥ before m becomes mṛtyor.
ā + a becomes ā: mā amṛtāt → māmṛtāt, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

morphology.note: After su-, gandha becomes gandhi: P. 5.4.135 (गन्धस्येदुत्पूतिसुसुरभिभ्यः). Hence sugandhi, ‘well-scented’.

Aorist optative (precative) middle, first singular, of √muc: ‘may I be freed’. The commentator glosses it with a plural, «मुक्षीमहि मुक्ता भवेम», and explains the singular as an interchange of number.
Here mā negates the second ablative: ‘from death, not from immortality’. The commentator: «अमृतान्मोक्षान्मा मुक्षोमहि न वियुज्यामहे» — let us not be parted from immortality, that is, release.

translation.literal: We worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. Like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be released from death, not from immortality.
translation.readable: We worship the three-eyed lord, fragrant, who makes all things thrive. As a ripe cucumber comes away from its stem, may I be freed from death, but not from the deathless.

anvaya: सुगन्धिम् पुष्टिवर्धनम् त्र्यम्बकम् यजामहे । उर्वारुकम् बन्धनात् इव मृत्योः मुक्षीय अमृतात् मा [मुक्षीय] ।
syntax: A first person plural statement of worship (yajāmahe) with an object and two epithets; then a first person singular wish (mukṣīya) with two ablatives, the first affirmed (mṛtyoḥ), the second negated (mā amṛtāt), and a simile (urvārukam iva bandhanāt) placed before them.

ambiguities.note: ‘Not from immortality’: the release asked for is from death only. The commentator glosses amṛta as release, «अमृतान्मोक्षान्मा मुक्षोमहि न वियुज्यामहे».

The commentator takes the fruit as ripe and falling easily, «यथोर्वरुकं कर्कट्यादेः फलं पक्कं सद्बन्धनाट्वृन्तादनायासेन मुच्यते» (his text writes urvaruka): release without struggle, as of ripeness. The verse itself does not say ‘ripe’.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: As printed 15 + 17 syllables: tryambakaṃ yajāmahe (7) sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam (8); urvārukam iva bandhanān (9) mṛtyor mukṣīya māmṛtāt (8). The first pāda has seven (tryambakam read with tri- as two syllables would give eight) and the third nine; the edition reports the counts and does not emend.

beginner: This is one of the best known verses of the Veda. It worships the "three-eyed" god, the commentator says the lord who is Pārvatī’s husband, calling him fragrant and the one who makes things grow and thrive. Then it asks for one thing with a striking image: as a ripe cucumber comes away from the vine without effort, may I be freed from death — but not from the deathless. The commentator explains "the deathless" as release itself: the speaker asks to be loosed from death and never separated from immortality. In this Upaniṣad the verse stands among the short prayers and offering formulas near its end. The edition reports what the verse and the commentator say; it makes no claim about what reciting it does for health or life.
analogy: Like a ripe fruit that falls from the vine at a touch: no tearing, only a letting go that comes from ripeness.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: We worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be released from death, not from immortality.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator addresses the god as the lord of Pārvatī, «हे भगवन्पार्वतीपते त्वां यजामहे», and glosses tryambaka as three-eyed, «त्र्यम्बकं त्रिनेत्रम्». ‘Fragrant’ is the fragrance of his divine body, smelt from afar like that of the ketakī flower: «यथा केतक्यादिसौगन्ध्यं दूरादाघ्रायते तथा तदीयदिव्यदेहसौरभ्यं सोऽयं सुगन्धिः». The release from death is asked for after worshipping him through rites such as the sandhyā worship, and the immortality not to be lost is release itself, «अमृतान्मोक्षान्मा मुक्षोमहि न वियुज्यामहे».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among them). The anonymous bhāṣya explains the words and the rite; it does not argue an Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita position here, so the edition gives none.

contemporary.text: The verse does not ask never to die; it asks that the parting from death be like ripe fruit leaving the vine — natural, unforced — and that nothing deathless be lost in it. It holds acceptance and hope in one image. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What in your own life would you like to let go of as easily as ripe fruit leaves the vine?
reflect.deeper: The verse asks for release from death but ‘not from immortality’. What does that second half add to the first?
reflect.practice: Notice one attachment that has become ‘ripe’ — no longer needed — and let it go without forcing.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 52–57 are missing from the digital text used here, and neither commentary file glosses these words; the edition’s concordance maps give no anuvāka of theirs for it. The anonymous bhāṣya is the only commentary quoted.
The verse is also in the Ṛgveda (7.59.12). The edition’s Ṛgveda source has only the first maṇḍala, so the parallel is noted here, not quoted.

flags.note: The identification of the three-eyed one as the lord of Pārvatī is the commentator’s; the verse itself names him only as tryambaka.
